name: 7 Powers Framework
description: Finds which of seven sources of durable advantage (Scale Economies, Network Economies, Counter-Positioning, Switching Costs, Branding, Cornered Resource, Process Power) a company has or can build.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when setting long-term business strategy, evaluating moat strength, or proving persistent defensibility and economic returns to investors.
inputs: Business model, value proposition, and revenue generation mechanisms
Company lifecycle stage (Origination, Takeoff, or Stability)
Main incumbents and emerging competitors
Unit economics and fixed vs. variable cost behavior with scale
questions: Do fixed costs spread over higher volume reduce per-unit costs faster than competitors can match?
Does the product's value to each user increase as the total network of users expands?
Is the company pursuing a superior business model that incumbents cannot copy without damaging their core business?
What financial, operational, or emotional costs do customers incur by switching to an alternative?
Does the brand command higher pricing or conversion for an otherwise identical offering due to trust?
Does the business hold exclusive, permanent access to a valuable asset, talent, patent, or resource?
Has the company developed embedded operational process complexities that yield superior quality or cost structures over time?
output: An assessment of present and latent powers across the business model, paired with a staged strategic roadmap to build at least one durable power before market arbitrage occurs.

name: AARRR Pirate Metrics
description: Breaks the customer lifecycle into Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, and Revenue to locate funnel friction and drive growth initiatives.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when diagnosing slow growth in digital or SaaS products, or aligning cross-functional growth teams around the leaky stages of the user lifecycle.
inputs: Channel acquisition performance and Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
User onboarding flows and activation milestone triggers
Cohort retention analysis curves over 30/60/90 days
Referral loop mechanics, viral coefficients, and LTV/pricing metrics
questions: Acquisition: Which channels drive high-intent users efficiently?
Activation: What specific action signals that a user experienced their initial 'Aha!' moment?
Retention: What percentage of users stay active over time, and where does cohort decay flatten out?
Referral: Do active users refer others, and what is the viral loop factor?
Revenue: How effectively do active users transition into paying accounts?
Which stage of the lifecycle exhibits the largest drop-off and represents the primary bottleneck to growth?
output: A lifecycle funnel conversion dashboard identifying the top growth bottleneck, supported by a prioritized backlog of growth hypotheses and experiments.

name: Ansoff Matrix
description: Categorizes growth strategies across four quadrants (Market Penetration, Market Development, Product Development, and Diversification) based on existing vs. new products and markets.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when evaluating growth paths, setting corporate revenue targets, and balancing risk profiles between core expansion and new ventures.
inputs: Current product portfolio and customer segment penetration rates
Growth targets, capital availability, and execution timeframe
Addressable market sizing and expansion capabilities
Corporate risk tolerance and R&D/GTM capacity
questions: Can growth targets be achieved by increasing market share of existing products in current markets (Market Penetration)?
Can existing products be introduced into new geographic areas, verticals, or demographics (Market Development)?
Can new products or features be developed to sell to our existing customer base (Product Development)?
Should the business introduce new products into entirely new markets, and what risk does this entail (Diversification)?
Which path offers the optimal balance of return on investment versus execution risk?
output: A categorized portfolio of growth options mapped by risk profile, complete with prioritized allocation of capital, resources, and validation milestones.

name: Balanced Scorecard
description: Translates high-level strategy into actionable performance goals across four distinct perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Processes, and Learning & Growth.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when leadership needs a balanced operational view that connects long-term organizational capabilities and process health directly to financial outcomes.
inputs: Corporate strategy and financial metrics
Customer satisfaction, retention, and value proposition targets
Operational workflow data and critical process performance
Employee capabilities, culture, and infrastructure status
questions: Financial: To succeed financially, how should we appear to our shareholders?
Customer: To achieve our vision, how should we appear to our customers?
Internal Processes: To satisfy our shareholders and customers, at what business processes must we excel?
Learning & Growth: To achieve our vision, how will we sustain our ability to change and improve?
What cause-and-effect linkages connect performance across these four dimensions?
output: A Strategy Map linking objectives across all four perspectives, paired with an integrated performance scorecard of metrics, targets, and strategic initiatives.

name: BCG Growth-Share Matrix
description: Classifies products or business units by relative market share and market growth rate into Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks, and Dogs to optimize portfolio resource allocation.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when managing a multi-product portfolio or business unit structure to allocate limited capital, attention, and cash flows rationally.
inputs: Complete inventory of products, services, or business units
Relative market share metrics (compared to leading market competitors)
Market growth rate data per category
Revenue, contribution margin, and cash generation/consumption profiles per unit
questions: Which offerings operate in rapidly growing markets and hold dominant market share (Stars)?
Which mature products generate steady cash flows well beyond their reinvestment needs (Cash Cows)?
Which offerings in high-growth markets have low market share and consume heavy cash with uncertain outcomes (Question Marks)?
Which products exhibit weak market share in stagnant or declining markets (Dogs)?
How can cash generated from Cash Cows be deployed to convert Question Marks into Stars?
Which underperforming products or business units should be harvested or divested?
output: A portfolio matrix mapping each unit into a quadrant, accompanied by clear capital allocation directives: Invest, Maintain/Hold, Harvest, or Divest.

name: Blue Ocean Strategy (Four Actions & Canvas)
description: Seeks to create uncontested market space and render competition irrelevant by simultaneously pursuing differentiation and low cost through Value Innovation.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when competing in hyper-competitive, commoditized markets ('red oceans') with shrinking margins and high acquisition costs.
inputs: Industry competitive factors (pricing, features, support, tech, service levels)
Relative performance ratings of core industry players
Customer pain points, friction, and non-customer demographics
Internal cost structures and operational levers
questions: Which factors that the industry takes for granted should be eliminated entirely?
Which factors should be reduced well below the industry standard?
Which factors should be raised well above the industry standard?
Which factors should be created that the industry has never offered?
Which tier of non-customers are currently avoiding the industry, and what fundamental barriers block them?
Does the resulting Strategy Canvas reveal a distinct, focused, and compelling tag line?
output: An Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create (ERRC) grid, a Strategy Canvas comparing current vs. new Value Curves, and a validated value proposition unlocking new market demand.

name: Business Model Canvas
description: Maps the complete blueprint of how an enterprise creates, delivers, and captures value across nine integrated building blocks.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when assessing an existing business model, designing a new line of business, or evaluating how changes in one area impact operational viability.
inputs: Core value propositions, target customer segments, and channel strategies
Customer relationship types and key revenue mechanisms
Essential key activities, strategic assets, and partner networks
Cost structure components (fixed and variable)
questions: Who are our target customer segments, and what value proposition do we deliver to each?
Through which channels do we interact with, sell to, and support customers?
How do we generate revenue streams, and what is customer willingness to pay?
Which key activities and assets are mandatory to operate our value chain?
Who are key partners, and what dependencies exist?
What are the major cost drivers of this model?
output: A completed nine-block Business Model Canvas detailing interdependencies, operational risks, and priority assumptions for testing.

name: Crossing the Chasm
description: Guides technology products across the dangerous gap between early adopters (Visionaries) and the early majority (Pragmatists) by dominating a targeted niche beachhead.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when an innovative technology product achieves initial traction with tech enthusiasts but mainstream sales plateau.
inputs: Early customer characteristics, sales histories, and adoption motives
Candidate target niche market segments
Product status vs. 'Whole Product' requirements (integrations, support, partners)
questions: Which single, highly specific customer niche exhibits the most compelling, urgent problem?
What is required to deliver a complete 'Whole Product' solution that leaves zero risk for pragmatic buyers in that niche?
Who are the trusted references within this niche that will influence neighboring segments?
How can we position ourselves as the undisputed dominant leader in this specific beachhead segment?
Which adjacent segments should we target once the beachhead is secured?
output: A defined Beachhead Market choice, a Whole Product architecture blueprint, pragmatic positioning statements, and a sequential segment expansion plan.

name: Cynefin Framework
description: Categorizes problems into five decision contexts (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, and Confused) to match leadership action styles to situational reality.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when a team is stuck on a decision, arguing over method, or incorrectly applying best practices to dynamic, unpredictable problems.
inputs: Characteristics of the decision situation or crisis at hand
Level of predictability and cause-and-effect clarity
Historical precedents and expertise availability
questions: Is cause-and-effect clear to everyone (Clear: Sense - Categorize - Respond)?
Is cause-and-effect separated by time/space requiring expert analysis (Complicated: Sense - Analyze - Respond)?
Is cause-and-effect only visible in hindsight (Complex: Probe - Sense - Respond)?
Is there no cause-and-effect relationship discernible and immediate action is required (Chaotic: Act - Sense - Respond)?
Which domain does this challenge belong to, and are we misapplying standard practices?
output: Contextual domain classification with prescribed response modes (Apply Best Practice, Analyze, Conduct Safe-to-Fail Experiments, or Act to Stabilize).

name: Disruptive Innovation
description: Analyzes how simpler, lower-cost, or more accessible innovations start in low-end or new-market niches and steadily move upmarket to displace incumbents.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework to assess whether an emerging challenger poses an existential threat, or to structure a new product entry against entrenched market leaders.
inputs: Incumbent products, cost structures, and overserved/profitable customer tiers
Challenger offering attributes, cost advantages, and rate of technological improvement
Underserved or non-consuming customer demographics
questions: Are mainstream customers overserved by incumbents and paying for performance features they don't use?
Does a market segment of non-consumers exist who lack the money or skill to buy current industry offerings?
Does the new entrant start with a simpler, lower-margin business model that incumbents prefer to yield rather than defend?
Is the entrant's improvement trajectory fast enough to satisfy mainstream market demands over time?
output: A diagnostic evaluation of disruptive potential, paired with strategic response choices: spin off an autonomous unit, launch a low-end offering, or yield non-core tiers.

name: First Principles Thinking
description: Breaks complex problems down to fundamental truths and constraints, then builds novel solutions from the ground up without relying on analogies or conventional practices.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when existing industry practices are too costly, slow, or ineffective, or when seeking breakthrough innovation in a conventional category.
inputs: A strategic challenge, costly process, or entrenched industry practice
Empirical facts, underlying physics, economics, or technical constraints
questions: What is the precise problem we are trying to solve?
What claims about this problem are fundamental, verifiable facts versus inherited assumptions?
Why is the current solution structured this way, and which parts are merely convention?
If we built a solution from scratch using only fundamental truths, what would it look like?
What cheap experiment can validate the feasibility of this reconstructed solution?
output: A problem breakdown separating core truths from conventional assumptions, accompanied by radical alternative solutions and a validation experiment design.

name: Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)
description: Analyzes customer demand around the fundamental progress a person is trying to make in a specific circumstance, rather than relying on static demographics or feature preferences.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when designing new products, refining value propositions, evaluating churn/switching behaviors, or uncovering hidden non-traditional competitors.
inputs: Customer interview data focused on recent purchase or cancellation decisions
Triggers, circumstances, and push/pull forces surrounding adoption
Workarounds and alternative solutions currently 'hired' by users
questions: What specific circumstance or trigger caused the customer to seek a new solution?
What functional, emotional, and social progress is the customer trying to achieve?
What existing tools or behaviors were they using, and what made them unsatisfactory?
What anxieties, habits, or switching costs created friction during adoption?
What other solutions, including doing nothing, compete for the same job?
output: A series of Job Statements outlining customer circumstances, desired outcomes, push/pull forces, and an actionable roadmap for product design and messaging.

name: Lean Canvas
description: A startup-focused adaptation of the Business Model Canvas prioritizing early-stage risk: Problems, Solutions, Key Metrics, and Unfair Advantage.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when evaluating early-stage startup ideas, defining initial business hypotheses, or designing rapid experiments prior to building product.
inputs: Target early adopter profiles and observed customer friction
Top customer problems and current alternatives
Proposed solution capabilities and pricing concepts
questions: What are the top 3 critical problems experienced by our target early adopters?
How do early adopters solve these problems today (existing alternatives)?
What simple, high-value solution features address these problems directly?
What single, clear Unique Value Proposition explains why we are different and worth attention?
What Unfair Advantage does the business possess that cannot be easily copied or bought?
What single key metric best indicates that value is being delivered?
Which assumption, if wrong, completely invalidates the concept?
output: A one-page Lean Canvas prioritizing core hypotheses, an initial unit economic outline, and a staged validation roadmap.

name: McKinsey 7-S Framework
description: Diagnoses organizational effectiveness and alignment across seven internal elements: the hard S's (Strategy, Structure, Systems) and the soft S's (Shared Values, Style, Staff, Skills).
whenToUse: Reach for this framework during strategic pivots, reorganizations, corporate mergers, or when strategy execution stalls despite a sound strategic plan.
inputs: Strategy documents and organizational reporting structures
Core operating systems, IT infrastructure, and formal processes
Cultural values, leadership style behaviors, talent baseline, and skills inventory
questions: Strategy: Is our strategy clear, and do all elements reinforce it?
Structure: Does the organizational hierarchy support or impede strategic goals?
Systems: Do operational processes and tools monitor and support execution?
Shared Values: What core beliefs unify the culture, and do they align with strategic needs?
Style: How do leaders make decisions, communicate, and manage?
Staff: Do we have the right talent pool in key positions?
Skills: What institutional competencies exist, and where are critical gaps?
Where are these seven elements out of alignment with one another?
output: A diagnostic report illustrating internal alignment gaps across the 7 elements, accompanied by an integrated organizational change implementation plan.

name: North Star Metric Framework
description: Identifies a single key metric that best reflects core customer value delivery and drives sustainable long-term revenue, supported by actionable input metrics.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when cross-functional teams are pulling in opposing directions or optimizing vanity metrics instead of real value creation.
inputs: Product usage analytics, feature engagement data, and retention drivers
Key customer outcomes and value indicators
Financial revenue drivers and subscription dynamics
questions: What specific user action proves that a customer received core value from our product?
Does growth in this metric directly lead to sustained retention and long-term revenue?
Can cross-functional teams directly influence this metric through product and marketing levers?
What 3–5 input metrics directly drive this North Star Metric?
What guardrail metrics must be monitored to ensure we don't optimize this metric in ways that harm the business?
output: A defined North Star Metric, an input metric hierarchy for product teams, guardrail measures, and an operational dashboard structure.

name: Objectives and Key Results (OKRs)
description: Connects ambitious organizational goals with 3–5 measurable, outcome-based Key Results to maintain focus and align execution.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework during quarterly or annual planning cycles to operationalize strategy and align focus across interdependent teams.
inputs: High-level strategic goals, vision, and operational priorities
Historical baseline metrics and KPI data
Team operational bandwidth, dependencies, and capacity constraints
questions: What key qualitative achievement will yield the highest strategic impact over the upcoming period (Objective)?
What 3–5 quantitative outcomes will conclusively prove that this Objective was realized (Key Results)?
What baseline values are we starting from, and what aggressive targets represent success?
What non-essential initiatives must be explicitly deprioritized to guarantee focus?
Which team and individual owners hold accountability for each Key Result?
output: A set of aligned Objectives paired with 3–5 quantifiable Key Results per objective, accompanied by baseline/target metrics, clear ownership assignments, and a review cadence.

name: PESTEL Analysis
description: Scans macro-environmental forces (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) to uncover key external drivers, risks, and strategic opportunities.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when entering a new geography or market, planning over a multi-year horizon, or checking whether outside macro forces have shifted underneath the current strategy.
inputs: Geographic markets and industries the company operates in or is evaluating
Target customer demographics and buying behaviors
Company business model, key cost drivers, and strategic horizon
Relevant economic trends, inflation/interest indicators, and exchange dynamics
Applicable regulatory, environmental, and trade policies
Emerging technological advancements and societal shifts
questions: Which current or upcoming laws, political decisions, or trade regulations could alter how we operate or sell?
How would macroeconomic shifts (recession, interest rate changes, inflation) impact customer spending?
Which demographic, cultural, or behavioral shifts make our product more or less essential to society?
Which emerging technologies could make our offering obsolete, cheaper to copy, or radically more efficient?
What environmental or sustainability expectations are customers, regulators, or investors holding us to?
Which external factors carry the highest likelihood and potential operational impact?
What strategic actions or pivots should the business execute in response?
output: A categorized assessment of external macro factors rated by likelihood and impact, highlighting emerging opportunities/threats alongside actionable strategic responses.

name: Playing to Win (Strategy Choice Cascade)
description: Defines strategy as an integrated set of five choices: Winning Aspiration, Where to Play, How to Win, Core Capabilities, and Management Systems.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework to transform high-level vision into concrete strategic choices, or when a business needs to make explicit trade-offs on where not to play.
inputs: Corporate mission, purpose, and financial targets
Market segments, geographies, channels, and product categories
Internal capabilities, cost drivers, and competitive advantages
Customer willingness to pay and economics
questions: What does winning look like for this enterprise (concrete, customer-focused ambition)?
Where will we play (specific customer segments, channels, geographies, product lines) and explicitly not play?
How will we win in those chosen areas (low-cost structure or differentiation leadership)?
What set of interconnected capabilities must be built and maintained to win there?
What management systems, metrics, and structures must support those capabilities?
What would have to be true for this set of strategic choices to be successful?
output: A one-page Strategy Cascade document outlining the 5 reinforced choices, explicit trade-offs/exclusions, and key underlying assumptions to validate.

name: Porter's Five Forces
description: Analyzes the five competitive forces (rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power, and supplier power) to determine industry attractiveness and persistent margin pressures.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when evaluating market entry, launching a net-new product category, assessing long-term profitability under shifting conditions, or identifying structural sources of competitive advantage.
inputs: Industry definition, geographic scope, and value chain profit margins
Main competitors, market concentration rates, and relative market shares
Key buyer segments, concentration rates, and switching costs
Key supplier concentration, platform dependencies, and input costs
Availability, cost-performance trade-offs, and switching ease of substitute products
Capital requirements, regulatory barriers, and structural entry barriers
questions: How intense is price competition and product differentiation among existing industry rivals?
What financial, structural, or regulatory barriers prevent well-funded newcomers from entering the market?
What viable non-industry alternative solutions exist, and how easily could customers switch to them?
How much leverage do key buyer segments hold over pricing, customization, and contract terms?
How strong is supplier concentration, and how much power do suppliers hold over key input costs?
Which of these forces exert the greatest pressure on industry margins, and which are strengthening or weakening over time?
Where can the company position itself to shield its business from the strongest competitive forces?
output: An industry profitability and structure assessment rating each force's strength with empirical evidence, identifying key margin risks, and delivering strategic positioning recommendations to minimize competitive pressures.

name: Pre-Mortem Analysis
description: Mitigates overconfidence and groupthink by assuming a proposed plan has failed catastrophically before launch, prompting the team to identify risks proactively.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework prior to finalizing a major strategy, product launch, M&A deal, or organizational restructuring.
inputs: Comprehensive plan details, launch milestones, goals, and timeline
Cross-functional team members involved in design and execution
questions: Imagine we are 12–24 months in the future, and this initiative has failed catastrophically. What went wrong?
Which customer, technical, competitive, or operational assumptions proved fatally incorrect?
What early warning signals did we overlook or ignore during execution?
Which identified failure modes carry the highest probability and impact?
What preventative adjustments or contingency plans must we incorporate into the live plan today?
output: A prioritized risk register mapping plausible failure causes, early warning indicators, preventative mitigations, and pre-planned decision triggers.

name: RICE Prioritization
description: Ranks competing features, projects, or strategic initiatives using four quantitative factors: Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when product or engineering teams face a long list of candidate initiatives and need an objective, standardized ranking methodology.
inputs: List of proposed features, projects, or experiments
Target audience size metrics (Reach)
Estimated effect on target goals (Impact)
Supporting data and evidence levels (Confidence)
Implementation resource requirements (Effort)
questions: Reach: How many users/customers will this initiative impact over a given time period?
Impact: How much will this increase our core metric for each user reached (0.25=Minimal, 1=Medium, 3=Massive)?
Confidence: How confident are we in our Reach and Impact estimates based on available evidence (100%=High, 80%=Medium, 50%=Low)?
Effort: How many person-months will be required across engineering, design, and GTM to complete this?
What is the final calculated RICE Score: (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort?
output: A scored and prioritized initiative backlog with explicit confidence weights, rationale, and recommended resource allocations.

name: Scenario Planning
description: Constructs multiple plausible future environments based on critical uncertainties to build resilient strategies and stress-test strategic choices.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework during times of severe macro, technological, or regulatory volatility when relying on a single forecast is dangerous.
inputs: Core decision question and target planning timeline
Macro-environmental trends and industry forces
Key driving forces categorized by impact and uncertainty
questions: What fundamental forces and trends will shape our operating environment over the target timeline?
Which two driving forces possess the highest potential impact and the highest degree of uncertainty?
What 4 distinct plausible scenario worlds emerge when plotting these two uncertainties on a 2x2 matrix?
How resilient is our current business model and strategy in each of these scenario worlds?
What no-regret strategic choices create value regardless of which scenario unfolds?
What early-warning indicators signal which scenario world is becoming reality?
output: Four distinct scenario narratives, a strategy stress-test assessment matrix, a list of 'no-regret' strategic moves, and early-warning monitoring signposts.

name: SWOT Analysis
description: Evaluates internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats to ground strategy in an honest situation assessment and establish strategic priorities.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework during initial strategy formulation, annual planning, before a major decision, or when synthesizing findings from other strategic analyses into a shared situational baseline.
inputs: Current company performance metrics, core competencies, and operational capabilities
Products, services, business model, and strategic objectives
Customer feedback, retention data, and performance benchmarks
Industry benchmarks, competitor landscape, and market trends
Macro-environmental factors (regulatory, technological, economic)
questions: What advantages, unique resources, or capabilities does the company possess that customers value over alternatives?
Where are current operational bottlenecks, resource gaps, or competitive vulnerabilities that cause lost deals or people?
What emerging market trends, technological shifts, or unserved customer needs present new avenues for growth?
What external shifts, market dynamics, or competitive moves could imperil current revenue or business operations?
Which strengths can be directly leveraged to capture the most attractive opportunities?
Which weaknesses leave the company most exposed to critical external threats?
Which top 3 strategic issues deserve immediate executive attention?
output: A structured SWOT matrix pairing internal capabilities with external dynamics, resulting in a prioritized list of strategic initiatives to capitalize on strengths, address weaknesses, and mitigate threats.

name: The Kernel of Good Strategy
description: Distills strategy down to its fundamental structure: a clear Diagnosis of the challenge, a Guiding Policy, and a set of Coherent Actions.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when strategy documents read like a collection of wishful goals, financial targets, or disjointed tactical lists rather than a focused plan of action.
inputs: Current organizational performance, systemic bottlenecks, and market obstacles
Existing operational plans, goals, and resource constraints
Feedback from frontline teams on execution roadblocks
questions: What is the single critical challenge or barrier standing in the company's path?
Why is this challenge hard, and what underlying forces perpetuate it?
What overarching Guiding Policy or approach will we adopt to address this diagnosis?
What specific, coordinated Coherent Actions will carry out this policy?
What competing initiatives or goals must we stop pursuing to concentrate energy on this challenge?
output: A concise strategy document identifying the core Diagnosis, the unifying Guiding Policy, and a set of mutually reinforcing Coherent Actions.

name: Three Horizons of Growth
description: Balances organizational focus and capital allocation across defending the core business (Horizon 1), scaling emerging opportunities (Horizon 2), and seeding long-term innovation (Horizon 3).
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when a business risks over-focusing on short-term optimization at the expense of future disruption, or vice versa.
inputs: Core business performance, margins, and decay curves
Pipeline of emerging business initiatives and early experiments
R&D budget, talent distribution, and long-term strategic ambition
questions: What critical initiatives are required in the next 0–12 months to optimize and defend our core revenue engines (Horizon 1)?
Which emerging initiatives could scale into high-margin revenue drivers in 1–3 years (Horizon 2)?
What high-upside options or disruptive bets should we seed for 3–5 years out (Horizon 3)?
How is leadership attention, budget, and talent distributed across these three horizons today versus where it should be?
Are we managing each horizon with metrics and management styles appropriate to its maturity?
output: A strategic portfolio map categorizing initiatives into three time horizons, complete with target resource ratios (e.g., 70/20/10) and distinct governance metrics for each.

name: TOWS Matrix
description: Extends SWOT analysis by systematically matching internal Strengths and Weaknesses with external Opportunities and Threats to generate distinct tactical strategy options.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework immediately following a SWOT analysis to transform descriptive lists into actionable, strategic options.
inputs: Prioritized lists of Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats from SWOT
Company strategic objectives, resource limits, and execution constraints
questions: How can we deploy internal Strengths to capitalize on external Opportunities (SO Strategies)?
How can we leverage Opportunities to overcome or bypass internal Weaknesses (WO Strategies)?
How can we use internal Strengths to protect against or mitigate external Threats (ST Strategies)?
How can we minimize internal Weaknesses and avoid severe exposure to external Threats (WT Strategies)?
Which combinations yield the highest strategic return given current capabilities?
output: A TOWS Matrix generating four explicit strategic action lists (SO, WO, ST, WT) prioritized by fit, impact, and feasibility.

name: Value Chain Analysis
description: Examines primary and support activities across the value chain to locate cost drivers, identify differentiation sources, and inform outsourcing decisions.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when looking for operational efficiency, margin expansion, product differentiation, or determining core vs. non-core activities.
inputs: Step-by-step workflow from inbound logistics to after-sales support
Activity-based cost accounting data and resource usage
Customer willingness-to-pay drivers and competitive benchmarks
questions: What are the primary activities (Inbound, Operations, Outbound, Marketing/Sales, Service) that create our product/service?
What support activities (Infrastructure, HR, Tech, Procurement) enable those primary steps?
Which specific activities account for the largest proportion of total operating costs?
In which activities do we create distinctive value that customers recognize and pay a premium for?
Which non-core activities could be performed better, faster, or cheaper by specialized external partners?
output: A Value Chain Map breaking down costs and value contributions per activity, paired with operational optimization and outsourcing recommendations.

name: Value Proposition Canvas
description: Zooms in on the Business Model Canvas to systematically match product Pain Relievers and Gain Creators directly with customer Jobs, Pains, and Gains.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when refining product-market fit, troubleshooting low conversion/retention, or positioning new feature additions.
inputs: Defined customer segment profiles and behavioral research
Observed customer tasks, frustrations, and aspirations
Existing or planned product feature specifications
questions: What functional, social, and emotional jobs is the customer trying to accomplish?
What severe pains, risks, or roadblocks do customers encounter while attempting these jobs?
What positive gains, outcomes, or delights do customers expect or desire?
How precisely do our product features act as pain relievers?
How do our product features produce the exact gains customers care about most?
output: A detailed Customer Profile and Value Map alignment diagram identifying high-fit features, messaging angles, and critical gaps in customer value.

name: VRIO Framework
description: Evaluates whether a company's internal resources and capabilities are Valuable, Rare, Inimitable, and Organized to capture value, identifying sources of sustained competitive advantage.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when the company needs to pinpoint its defensible competitive advantages before choosing where to invest capital, expand positioning, or protect against fast followers.
inputs: Key internal resources: technology, proprietary data, brand, talent, processes, partnerships
Competitor assets, capabilities, and market positions
Evidence of customer value, utility, and willingness to pay
Organizational governance structure, capital allocation, and operating processes
questions: Which assets or capabilities enable the business to exploit market opportunities or neutralize threats?
Which of these valuable resources are possessed by few or no competing players?
How difficult, expensive, or time-consuming would it be for competitors to imitate or substitute these capabilities?
Is the company structured, funded, and managed to fully exploit these resources?
Which capabilities provide only parity or temporary advantage, and which offer a defensible, sustained advantage?
Where should the firm allocate resources to reinforce its most defensible advantage?
output: A matrix classifying each core resource as a competitive disadvantage, parity, temporary advantage, or sustained competitive advantage, paired with actionable recommendations on capital allocation and defense.

name: Wardley Mapping
description: Maps component value chains according to user needs along an evolutionary continuum (Genesis, Custom, Product, Commodity) to inform build/buy/outsource strategies.
whenToUse: Reach for this framework when making architectural, build-versus-buy, or supply chain decisions, or when anticipating market component commoditization.
inputs: Anchor user profiles and their explicit high-level needs
Complete chain of dependent technologies, activities, and practices
Market maturity state of each component in the ecosystem
questions: Who is the target user, and what primary need anchors this value chain?
What sub-components, services, and infrastructure are required to deliver that need?
Where does each component lie on the evolutionary axis (Genesis, Custom, Product, Commodity)?
Are we spending engineering resources custom-building components that have become standardized products or commodities?
Which components are evolving rapidly, and what strategic moves can we execute to exploit that movement?
output: A visual Wardley Map of the value chain displaying component evolution, identifying strategic waste, and highlighting high-leverage build/buy/outsource actions.
